# Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation

###### Abstract

Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are
increasingly applied to scientific discovery and hypothesis generation.
Both the effect of refinement and the diversity of the delivered set are
hard to interpret before experimental ground truth exists, and both are
typically reported by deciding, for pairs of generated hypotheses,
whether they describe the same underlying mechanism. We study two
evaluation questions that rest on this pairwise equivalence judgment:
(1) how much self-critique changes delivered hypotheses beyond
run-to-run variability, and (2) how the equivalence rule used to group
hypotheses affects measured diversity. Our study workflow generates
mechanistic explanations represented as causal chains from a molecular
initiating event through intermediate biological steps to an observed
outcome, revised through self-critique rounds before a final
consolidation step. Across four independent proprietary instances, we
hold opening hypotheses fixed, rerun the downstream workflow with 0, 1,
and 5 critique rounds, and score matched hypothesis pairs with an
LLM-as-a-judge. Relative to matched same-depth reruns, moving from 0 to
1 round produces 34.5 percentage points (pp) of additional
mechanism-level divergence, whereas 1 to 5 rounds adds 1.3 pp. We then
compare three equivalence rules: term frequency–inverse document
frequency (TF–IDF) similarity, dense embeddings, and the same
LLM-as-a-judge. To characterize how these rules respond to specific
edits, we construct controlled hypothesis pairs that either alter only
wording or equivalent biological terminology while preserving the causal
explanation, or replace one component of the causal chain while holding
the remaining structure fixed. All three rules are invariant to
meaning-preserving edits, but when the initiating event is replaced, the
LLM-as-a-judge identifies 83% of valid pairs as different mechanisms,
versus 0% for TF–IDF and 8% for embeddings; varying only the rubric that
defines same mechanism moves this figure from 38% to 96%. Together,
these results show that pairwise equivalence judgments are a measurement
choice: how mechanism equivalence is defined affects both the estimated
effect of self-critique and the measured diversity of generated
hypotheses.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being incorporated into
scientific workflows, where agentic systems propose and refine
hypotheses ([Gottweis et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Ghareeb et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)), interpret experimental data ([Huang and others,
2025](#bib.bib15); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)), design candidate
molecules ([Bran et al., 2024](#bib.bib17); [Swanson et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14)), and plan follow-up experiments ([Huang and others,
2025](#bib.bib15)). Evaluating such systems departs from the standard
benchmark setting. Scientific hypotheses often concern mechanisms whose
truth is not yet established when they are proposed, and the experiments
required to adjudicate them can be expensive and time-consuming.
Correctness therefore becomes available, if at all, only after the
system must already be evaluated, necessitating evaluation criteria that
can be applied directly to the generated hypotheses.

In the absence of such an external signal, recent systems evaluate
generated hypotheses by comparing them with one another, both while
refining candidates and when reporting the delivered set. The AI
co-scientist ranks hypotheses through an Elo tournament of pairwise
scientific debates, and separately consolidates its output set by
clustering hypotheses in an embedding-based proximity graph ([Gottweis
et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)). Robin ranks candidates by asking an
LLM-as-a-judge which of two hypotheses is better across all pairs and
fitting a Bradley–Terry–Luce model to the outcomes ([Ghareeb et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)). [Si et al. (2025)](#bib.bib20) use both: generated
ideas are deduplicated by thresholding pairwise embedding similarity
before an LLM-as-a-judge orders the survivors. These systems apply
different comparison rules to different purposes, with LLM-based
preference judgments prioritizing candidates and embedding similarity
supporting deduplication.

Pairwise equivalence judgments provide a common measurement basis for
two evaluation questions that are otherwise treated separately. First,
assessing the effect of self-critique requires determining _how much the
delivered hypotheses change as critique depth varies_, relative to
run-to-run variability across repeated executions at the same critique
depth. Second, measuring the diversity of a generated set requires
determining _when two hypotheses should be treated as distinct
explanations_ rather than alternative formulations of the same
explanation. Although these questions concern different properties of
the workflow, both involve the same hypothesis comparison task of
deciding whether a pair should be treated as the same or different.

We study this problem in a multi-agent hypothesis generation workflow.
Given an unexpected experimental finding, the workflow proposes
mechanistic hypotheses that explain it, each represented as a causal
chain from an initiating event through intermediate biological steps to
that finding. For the first question, we hold the opening hypotheses
fixed and vary only critique depth, then read cross-depth divergence
against matched same-depth reruns, since repeating an identical
configuration also changes the delivered hypotheses ([Atil et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21)). For the second, no labels exist for whether two
generated hypotheses share a mechanism, so we compare equivalence rules
on constructed pairs whose intended relation is known: some edits
preserve the mechanism and should not change a rule’s verdict, while
others replace a component of the causal chain and should.

- •
  We identify the pairwise equivalence judgment—deciding whether two
  hypotheses are the same or different—as a shared measurement basis for
  two evaluation questions that are usually treated separately: what
  changes beyond same-condition run-to-run variability, and what counts
  as one mechanism when measuring diversity.
- •
  Replaying the downstream workflow from identical opening hypotheses,
  we show that the largest change in delivered mechanisms occurs when
  critique is first introduced: moving from 0 to 1 round produces 34.5
  pp of divergence beyond matched rerun variability, whereas moving from
  1 to 5 rounds adds 1.3 pp.
- •
  We audit three equivalence rules with controlled perturbations.
  TF–IDF, embeddings, and an LLM-as-a-judge behave alike on
  meaning-preserving edits, but diverge when the initiating event is
  replaced: the LLM-as-a-judge reads 83% of these pairs as different
  mechanisms, compared with 8% for embeddings and 0% for TF–IDF, and
  varying only the judge’s rubric moves this rate from 38% to 96%.

## 2 Related Work

#### LLM agents for scientific hypothesis generation.

LLM agents are now applied across the stages of a scientific workflow,
from interpreting experimental data and designing candidate molecules to
planning and executing experiments, and benchmarks have been built to
measure these capabilities ([Boiko et al., 2023](#bib.bib16); [Bran et
al., 2024](#bib.bib17); [Laurent et al., 2024](#bib.bib22); [Huang and
others, 2025](#bib.bib15); [Swanson et al., 2025](#bib.bib14); [Chen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib23)). Single-agent designs pursue it through
iteration, alternating between generation and self-evaluation modules
and reporting that self-evaluation improves the novelty and relevance of
proposals ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)). Multi-agent designs instead
distribute the same work across specialized roles: the AI co-scientist
separates generation, reflection, ranking, evolution, and
proximity-based consolidation ([Gottweis et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)),
Robin couples literature-grounded generation with experimental analysis
([Ghareeb et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)), and VirSci organizes a simulated
research team that generates, discusses, and assesses ideas before
selecting one ([Su et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)).

#### Self-critique and iterative refinement.

Refinement is a standard way to spend additional computation on a
candidate output before delivering it. A single agent can revise its own
output from model-generated feedback or environmental signals ([Madaan
et al., 2023](#bib.bib4); [Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib5)), and
multi-agent designs assign the critique to a separate instance that
challenges the proposal before a final response is produced ([Du et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6)). Test-time scaling studies place this sequential
revision alongside parallel sampling, aggregation, and verifier-based
merging as alternative ways to allocate the same inference budget, both
for LLMs and for the agents ([Byun et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Zhu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib24)). How much the added computation helps varies
with the setting: intrinsic self-correction without external feedback
can leave reasoning unimproved ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib18); [Kamoi
et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)) and debate does not always outperform simpler
ensembling ([Smit et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)). In each case the effect is
read against a gold answer or a task-specific metric, a reference that
open-ended hypothesis generation makes available only after the fact.

#### Comparative evaluation without a reference.

When an external reference is available, a generation can be scored
against it. FActScore decomposes text into atomic claims and assesses
their evidential support, while ALCE evaluates the correctness and
completeness of generated citations ([Min et al., 2023](#bib.bib8); [Gao
et al., 2023](#bib.bib9)). Without such a reference, evaluation compares
generations with one another, and the common instrument is a pairwise
LLM-as-a-judge that decides which of two outputs is better ([Zheng et
al., 2023](#bib.bib10); [Liusie et al., 2024](#bib.bib27)). Because no
reference is available for evaluating the LLM-as-a-judge itself,
responsible use requires understanding its behavior ([Shi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12); [Eiras et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)).

## 3 Problem Formulation: Evaluation without Experimental Ground Truth

Given an unexpected experimental finding, a generation run delivers a
set of mechanistic hypotheses $`\mathcal{H}=\{h_{1},\ldots,h_{n}\}`$
that could explain it, where each $`h_{i}`$ is a causal chain from an
initiating event through intermediate biological steps to that finding,
and $`n`$ varies across runs. Candidate hypotheses may be iteratively
revised through self-critique before the final set is produced. Because
the underlying biological mechanism is unknown at generation time, no
experimental ground truth is available for deciding whether a proposed
mechanism is correct. Such comparison requires an _equivalence rule_
$`\rho_{m}(h_{i},h_{j})\in\{0,1\}`$, indexed by the comparison method
$`m`$, that returns $`1`$ when two hypotheses express the same
mechanism.

#### What changes beyond run-to-run variability?

Write $`\mathcal{R}_{K}`$ for the set of runs performed with up to $`K`$
critique rounds. For a run $`r\in\mathcal{R}_{K}`$, let
$`\mathcal{H}_{r}`$ denote the set of hypotheses produced after
self-critique. To compare two runs $`r`$ and $`r^{\prime}`$, we form a
set of matched hypothesis pairs $`M(r,r^{\prime})`$, where each pair
$`(h,h^{\prime})`$ contains corresponding hypotheses from
$`\mathcal{H}_{r}`$ and $`\mathcal{H}_{r^{\prime}}`$. A blinded
LLM-as-a-judge supplies the equivalence rule here, with
$`\rho_{\mathrm{LLM}}(h,h^{\prime})\in\{0,1\}`$ assigning $`1`$ when the
pair describes the same mechanism and $`0`$ otherwise. We define the
_divergence_ between the two runs as the fraction of matched hypothesis
pairs judged to describe different mechanisms,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
D(r,r^{\prime})=\frac{1}{|M(r,r^{\prime})|}\sum_{(h,h^{\prime})\in M(r,r^{\prime})}\left[1-\rho_{\mathrm{LLM}}(h,h^{\prime})\right].
``` |  | (1) |

Here, $`|M(r,r^{\prime})|`$ is the number of matched hypothesis pairs
used to compare the two runs. Thus, $`D(r,r^{\prime})=0`$ when all
matched pairs are judged to describe the same mechanism, while larger
values indicate greater mechanism-level divergence between the two runs.

A cross-depth difference alone does not indicate how much of the
observed change is specific to critique depth, because rerunning the
same configuration can also produce different hypotheses. Let
$`\bar{D}_{K,K^{\prime}}`$ denote the mean divergence over run pairs
with critique depths $`K`$ and $`K^{\prime}`$, and let
$`\bar{D}^{\mathrm{within}}_{K,K^{\prime}}`$ denote the mean divergence
over all same-depth run pairs from the two configurations. We define the
*extra divergence* as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta(K,K^{\prime})=\bar{D}_{K,K^{\prime}}-\bar{D}^{\mathrm{within}}_{K,K^{\prime}},
``` |  | (2) |

with the opening hypotheses held fixed so that critique depth is the
only experimentally varied configuration. A positive
$`\Delta(K,K^{\prime})`$ indicates that runs at different critique
depths diverge more than expected from rerunning the corresponding
same-depth configurations, whereas $`\Delta(K,K^{\prime})=0`$ indicates
no additional divergence beyond this run-to-run variability.

#### What counts as one mechanism when measuring diversity?

Once hypotheses have been generated, reporting their diversity requires
grouping $`\mathcal{H}`$ into distinct mechanisms and counting the
resulting groups. Here $`m`$ ranges over the candidate comparison
methods—TF–IDF similarity, dense embeddings, and an LLM-as-a-judge—and
the same grouping procedure is applied to the pairwise decisions of
each,

|     |                                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{P}_{m}=\mathcal{P}\!\left(\mathcal{H};\rho_{m}\right),
       ```                                                              |     | (3) |

where $`\mathcal{P}`$ clusters $`\mathcal{H}`$ under $`\rho_{m}`$ and
returns the number of resulting clusters. Because no reference is
available for scoring $`\rho_{m}`$ either, we audit the candidate rules
with targeted perturbations: some preserve the underlying mechanism,
whereas others replace a specified component of the causal chain.

## 4 Experimental Setup

![Refer to caption](2610.04133v1/workflow_diagram.png)

Figure 1: Multi-agent workflow for mechanistic hypothesis generation
used in this study. An unexpected experimental finding initiates
evidence retrieval. Candidate hypotheses are generated in parallel and
iteratively refined through self-critique loops between proposer and
critic agents. The resulting hypotheses are then consolidated into a
final report.

We study our multi-agent workflow on four independent proprietary
instances, each defined by an unexpected experimental finding and its
retrieved evidence
(Figure [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation")).
The instances are proprietary and are anonymized as A–D throughout. For
each instance, we perform five independent hypothesis-generation and
refinement processes, using retrieved evidence and up to $`K`$ rounds of
self-critique before consolidation.

Generation and evaluation are kept separate: all evaluation is performed
post hoc and does not influence hypothesis generation or refinement.
Generation uses Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the proposer and critic. Two
judges are used post hoc, both Claude Opus 4.6 at temperature 0: one
labels how the proposer responds to each critique, and one applies the
equivalence rule that decides whether two hypotheses describe the same
mechanism. Dense representations use Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2.
The equivalence judgments are additionally repeated across three model
families (Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5) to assess
sensitivity. These models are used exclusively for post-hoc evaluation
and provide no feedback to the generation process.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Pairwise Mechanism Comparison Methods ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation")
provides the details.

## 5 Results

We first examine how changing critique depth alters the delivered
mechanisms relative to the run-to-run variability observed under the
same critique setting. We then examine how different equivalence rules
affect measured diversity by changing which generated hypotheses are
treated as distinct mechanisms.

### 5.1 Critique-depth effects relative to run-to-run variability

#### Critique is actively incorporated during refinement.

Across the critique exchanges from the four proprietary instances, a
blinded post-hoc LLM-as-a-judge decomposes the critiques into 332
individual demands and finds that 61% are conceded, 27% are answered, 9%
are partially addressed, and 3% are dropped. These results show that the
refinement process engages with the critiques, but do not establish how
much critique changes the final hypotheses or whether those changes are
scientifically beneficial.

#### Most critique-depth divergence appears after the first critique round.

Holding the opening hypotheses fixed, we replay the downstream process
with 0, 1, and 5 critique rounds and compare the resulting hypotheses
against matched same-depth reruns. All comparisons are conducted within
instance to account for differences in the number and composition of
generated hypotheses. The blinded LLM-as-a-judge is not given the
critique depth or provenance of either hypothesis.

Under the primary evaluator shown in
Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Most critique-depth divergence appears after the first critique round. ‣ 5.1 Critique-depth effects relative to run-to-run variability ‣ 5 Results ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation"),
same-depth reruns with no critique show 0% divergence for all four
instances, whereas reruns with 1 critique round show 58%–76% divergence
across instances. Although downstream generation and consolidation
remain stochastic, the zero-round condition is substantially
reproducible at the mechanism level. Relative to the corresponding
same-depth baselines, moving from 0 to 1 critique round produces 34.5
percentage points (pp) of extra divergence, whereas moving from 1 to 5
rounds adds 1.3 pp. Moving from 0 to 5 rounds produces 39.8 pp of extra
divergence. Thus, most of the cross-depth separation appears when
critique is first introduced, with little additional separation from
later rounds. This pattern is robust to evaluator choice: across three
evaluator configurations, the 0-to-1 extra divergence ranges from 34.5
to 37.3 pp, while the corresponding same-depth rerun ranges are 0%–5% at
zero critique and 58%–76% at one critique round
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Critique-Depth Effects Relative to Run-to-Run Variability ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation")).

Figure 2: Effect of critique depth relative to run-to-run variability.
(a) Divergence between same-depth reruns at 0, 1, and 5 critique rounds.
(b) Extra divergence when critique depth changes, measured relative to
the corresponding same-depth rerun variability. Most of the cross-depth
separation occurs when critique is first introduced (0 to 1 round), with
little additional separation from 1 to 5 rounds. Points show individual
instances and bars show the aggregate result across instances.

The preceding divergence estimates were obtained under a single
equivalence rule, implemented by an LLM-as-a-judge that determined
whether each matched pair described the same mechanism. Pairwise
equivalence judgments also underlie the measurement of output diversity.
When hypotheses are generated in parallel, estimating diversity requires
grouping hypotheses judged to express the same explanation, and the
resulting number of distinct groups may vary with the equivalence rule
used. We therefore compare three equivalence rules applied to the same
set of hypotheses.

### 5.2 Measured diversity depends on the equivalence rule

We compare three rules for deciding whether two generated hypotheses
describe the same mechanism. TF–IDF similarity scores a pair by weighted
lexical overlap, so that shared rare terms count for more than shared
common ones ([Jones, 1972](#bib.bib25)). Dense embedding similarity
replaces this surface match with cosine distance between learned
sentence representations, which can align paraphrases that share little
vocabulary ([Reimers and Gurevych, 2019](#bib.bib26)). An LLM-as-a-judge
is shown both hypotheses and returns a same-or-different verdict under a
written rubric ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)). We examine the
pairwise decisions directly, using controlled perturbations that either
preserve the underlying mechanism or alter a specified component of the
causal chain.

#### Targeted perturbations probe what each rule treats as a distinct mechanism.

Each hypothesis contains a natural language mechanistic explanation and
a causal chain from an initiating event through intermediate biological
steps to the observed findings. We construct four controlled variants,
each changing a specific aspect of the original hypothesis. Wording Only
rewrites the mechanistic explanation while leaving the causal chain
unchanged. Wording + Chain additionally rewrites the chain using audited
biological aliases while preserving the same entities and causal
structure. Both are designed to preserve the underlying mechanism. First
Step Swapped replaces the initiating event while keeping the downstream
structure fixed and is designed to represent a different mechanism under
our study definition. Middle Step Swapped replaces one intermediate
causal step while preserving the initiating event and terminal finding.
Details are included in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Controlled Perturbations for Grouping Decisions ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation").

#### Targeted perturbations reveal different rule sensitivities.

All three rules classify every valid Wording Only and Wording + Chain
pair as the same mechanism, indicating robustness to paraphrasing and
audited alias substitutions
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Explicit criteria improve sensitivity to causal differences. ‣ 5.2 Measured diversity depends on the equivalence rule ‣ 5 Results ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation")).
Differences emerge when the causal structure is altered. For First Step
Swapped, the LLM-as-a-judge classifies 83% of pairs as different,
compared with 0% for TF–IDF and 8% for embeddings, suggesting that
global similarity measures may be less sensitive when a single causally
important component changes while most of the hypothesis remains
unchanged. For Middle Step Swapped, the LLM-as-a-judge classifies only
13% of pairs as different, while TF–IDF and embeddings classify none as
different, indicating that even the LLM-as-a-judge often treats changes
to intermediate causal steps as variation within the same mechanism.
This motivates examining how the LLM-as-a-judge’s decisions change when
the evaluation rubric is specified differently.

#### LLM-as-a-judge behavior depends on prompt specification.

We test whether the LLM-as-a-judge’s same or different decisions depend
on how the evaluation criteria are specified. We compare three prompt
variants: the *full rubric* used throughout the paper, a *step-by-step*
rubric that separately evaluates the initiating event, causal route, and
terminal outcome before the overall verdict, and a *no-rubric* version
that provides only the comparison task and verdict field. All prompts
are provided in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E LLM-as-a-judge Prompts ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation").

#### Explicit criteria improve sensitivity to causal differences.

In
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Explicit criteria improve sensitivity to causal differences. ‣ 5.2 Measured diversity depends on the equivalence rule ‣ 5 Results ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation"),
all three prompts remain invariant to Wording Only and Wording + Chain
edits. The largest difference appears for First Step Swapped: the
no-rubric prompt classifies 38% of pairs as different, compared with 83%
under the full rubric and 96% under the step-by-step rubric. The
step-by-step rubric also increases sensitivity to Middle Step Swapped
changes, from 13% under the full rubric to 21%, while explicitly
separating judgments of the initiating event, causal route, and terminal
outcome. Reversing the presentation order changes decisions for 5.6% of
controlled perturbation pairs under each prompt variant, although the
affected controlled pairs differ across rubrics
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Sensitivity Analyses for Pairwise Comparison Methods ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation")).
Together, these results suggest that making the comparison criteria more
explicit helps the LLM-as-a-judge distinguish causally meaningful
differences while preserving invariance to meaning-preserving edits.

Figure 3: Responses to targeted perturbations. All three rules classify
Wording Only and Wording + Chain variants as the same mechanism. When
the causal chain changes: the LLM-as-a-judge is more sensitive to First
Step Swapped changes than TF–IDF or embeddings, while all three are less
sensitive to Middle Step Swapped changes.

Figure 4: Prompt specification changes the causal differences detected
by the LLM-as-a-judge. All three prompts remain invariant to Wording
Only and Wording + Chain edits, while more explicit criteria increase
sensitivity to causal changes: for First Step Swapped, the share
classified as different rises from 38% with no rubric to 83% with the
full rubric and 96% with the step-by-step rubric, which also increases
sensitivity to Middle Step Swapped changes.

## 6 Conclusion

We studied two questions for evaluating scientific hypothesis generation
before experimental ground truth is available: how much self-critique
changes delivered mechanisms beyond run-to-run variability, and how the
equivalence rule affects measured diversity. Moving from 0 to 1 critique
round produced 34.5 pp of extra divergence, whereas 1 to 5 rounds added
1.3 pp. Under controlled perturbations, all three rules were robust to
meaning-preserving edits but differed on causal changes: for First Step
Swapped, the LLM-as-a-judge read 83% of pairs as different, compared
with 8% for embeddings and 0% for TF–IDF, and this rate varied from 38%
to 96% with the rubric alone. These results suggest that evaluation
should account for variability and carefully consider both the
equivalence method and the rubric used to interpret measured diversity.

#### Limitations.

Our study is limited to four proprietary instances and five repetitions
per critique depth, and no biological ground truth is available for the
generated hypotheses. The results therefore characterize how the
workflow outputs and evaluation methods behave, rather than whether
critique improves scientific correctness or whether a particular
grouping corresponds to the biologically correct mechanism.

Our post-hoc evaluation also relies on repeated LLM-based comparisons,
which may become computationally expensive as the number of generated
hypotheses increases. Pairwise mechanism comparisons grow rapidly with
the size of the hypothesis set, while robustness analyses across judge
models and prompt variants introduce additional inference cost.

Finally, measured diversity remains sensitive to evaluator design.
TF–IDF and embedding results depend on similarity thresholds, while LLM
same or different judgments vary with judge model, prompt specification,
and presentation order
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Sensitivity Analyses for Pairwise Comparison Methods ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation")).
Because the judges and generators belong to the same broad class of
LLMs, agreement across judge families does not rule out shared biases
such as self-preference or sensitivity to superficial properties. Our
controlled perturbations also probe only a limited set of semantic and
causal changes. Broader, systematically constructed perturbation suites
and independently specified evaluation rubrics would provide stronger
evidence about which causal distinctions an evaluator captures and how
robustly it captures them.

#### Future work.

A first direction is to improve the efficiency of post-hoc evaluation,
for example through selective pairwise comparison, cascaded evaluators
that invoke an LLM-as-a-judge only for ambiguous pairs, or distillation
of LLM judgments into smaller models. A second direction is to
strengthen the evaluation reference itself. Blinded domain experts could
help validate controlled perturbations, refine the rubric for
distinguishing mechanisms, and adjudicate same/different decisions.
Measuring expert–expert and expert–model agreement across a broader
range of mechanistic differences would help identify where automated
evaluators are reliable and where their judgments remain ambiguous.
Ultimately, prospective experimental evidence will be needed to
determine whether critique-induced changes and evaluator-defined
distinctions correspond to scientifically meaningful biological
mechanisms.

## Appendix A Critique-Depth Effects Relative to Run-to-Run Variability

This analysis quantifies how much changing critique depth alters the
delivered mechanisms beyond the run-to-run variability observed when the
same critique setting is repeated. Holding the opening hypotheses fixed,
we replay the downstream workflow with 0, 1, and 5 critique rounds and
use a blinded LLM-as-a-judge to compare matched delivered hypotheses.
For each run pair, divergence $`D(r,r^{\prime})`$ is the proportion of
matched hypothesis pairs classified as different mechanisms. Extra
divergence $`\Delta(K,K^{\prime})`$ is the mean cross-depth divergence
minus the mean divergence between same-depth reruns at the corresponding
depths. Formal definitions are provided in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Formulation: Evaluation without Experimental Ground Truth ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation").

For each of instances A–D, one donor run provides five opening
hypotheses, which are held fixed across all replays while every
downstream stage is rerun. Each critique depth is repeated five times
per instance, yielding 15 runs per instance and 60 runs in total. The 15
runs produce 105 run-pair comparisons per instance and 420 across all
four instances, comprising 4,863 matched hypothesis pairs.

For each instance and each pairwise depth comparison, the five runs from
each depth are pooled, and all 126 unique partitions of the ten runs
into two groups of five are considered. We recompute $`\Delta`$ for each
partition, and the two-sided $`p`$ value is the proportion of partitions
that produce an absolute $`\Delta`$ at least as large as the observed
value. For the aggregate result, this permutation is performed
separately within each instance, after which the four instance-specific
$`\Delta`$ values are averaged.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | Same-Depth Rerun |  |  | Cross-Depth Difference |  |  |  |
|  | Divergence (%) |  |  | Extra divergence (pp) |  |  |  |
| Instance | $`K=0`$ | $`K=1`$ | $`K=5`$ | $`0\!\rightarrow\!1`$ | $`1\!\rightarrow\!5`$ | $`0\!\rightarrow\!5`$ | All Three |
| Instance A | $`0`$ | $`58`$ | $`63`$ | $`35.4`$ | $`-4.0`$ | $`42.3`$ | $`24.6`$ |

| Instance B | $`0`$ | $`76`$ | $`72`$ | $`40.1`$ | $`7.3`$ | $`42.1`$ | $`29.8`$ |
|  |  |  |  | .008 | .048 | .008 | $`<`$.001 |
| Instance C | $`0`$ | $`59`$ | $`57`$ | $`38.3`$ | $`2.1`$ | $`42.9`$ | $`27.8`$ |
|  |  |  |  | .008 | .587 | .008 | $`<`$.001 |
| Instance D | $`0`$ | $`75`$ | $`71`$ | $`24.2`$ | $`-0.1`$ | $`31.9`$ | $`18.7`$ |

Table 1: Cross-depth separation is concentrated in comparisons between
the no-critique condition and conditions with critique.
Instance-averaged extra divergence, measured relative to the
corresponding same-depth rerun divergence, is 34.5,pp for $`K=0`$ versus
$`K=1`$ and 39.8,pp for $`K=0`$ versus $`K=5`$, compared with 1.3,pp for
$`K=1`$ versus $`K=5`$. Gray entries report $`p`$ values.

#### Evaluator sensitivity.

Opus 4.6 serves as the primary LLM-as-a-judge throughout this study. To
assess whether the observed critique-depth pattern depends on the choice
of judge model, we repeat the comparison using Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, and
GPT-5.5. For each judge, we recompute extra divergence, defined as
cross-depth divergence relative to the corresponding same-depth rerun
variability.

All three judges produce the same qualitative pattern
(Figure [5](#A1.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Evaluator sensitivity. ‣ Appendix A Critique-Depth Effects Relative to Run-to-Run Variability ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation")).
The 0-to-1 comparison ranges from +34.5 to +37.3 pp of extra divergence,
and the 0-to-5 comparison ranges from +39.8 to +43.3 pp; both
comparisons are significant under every judge ($`p<0.0001`$). In
contrast, the 1-to-5 comparison ranges from +0.5 to +2.3 pp. Thus,
across these judges, most cross-depth separation appears when critique
is first introduced, with limited additional separation from later
rounds.

Figure 5: Sensitivity of extra divergence to the judge model. Extra
divergence is recomputed using Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, and GPT-5.5 under
the same evaluation criteria. Bars show extra divergence averaged across
Instances, whiskers indicate the minimum-to-maximum range of the four
instance-specific estimates, and annotations report two-sided
permutation $`p`$ values. Across the three judges, extra divergence
ranges from 34.5 to 37.3 pp for $`K=0`$ versus $`K=1`$ and from 39.8 to
43.3 pp for $`K=0`$ versus $`K=5`$, compared with 0.5 to 2.3 pp for
$`K=1`$ versus $`K=5`$.

## Appendix B Pairwise Mechanism Comparison Methods

We compare three methods for determining whether a pair of hypotheses
describes the same mechanism. Each method receives the same hypothesis
statement, mechanistic explanation, and causal chain. In our TF–IDF
implementation, vectors are constructed using sublinear term-frequency
scaling and English stopword removal; pairs with cosine similarity of at
least 0.25 are classified as the same mechanism. Dense embeddings are
generated using amazon.titan-embed-text-v2, with pairs classified as the
same mechanism when their cosine similarity is at least 0.77. This
threshold is selected by matching the marginal same-pair rate to the
range produced by the other methods, without using individual pair
decisions as labels. The LLM-as-a-judge evaluator uses
claude-opus-4-6-v1 at temperature 0 and directly returns a binary
same/different decision. The LLM-as-a-judge is queried three times per
pair, including one presentation-order reversal, and the majority
decision is used. The full presentation-order sensitivity is examined in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Sensitivity Analyses for Pairwise Comparison Methods ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation"),
and evaluation rubric and its two prompt variants are in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E LLM-as-a-judge Prompts ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation").

## Appendix C Controlled Perturbations for Grouping Decisions

#### Perturbation definitions.

Each perturbation pair consists of one generated hypothesis and one
edited variant designed to test how the comparison methods respond to a
specific change. Wording Only rewrites the mechanistic explanation while
leaving the causal chain unchanged, whereas Wording + Chain also
rewrites the chain using audited biological aliases while preserving the
ordered entities and causal relations. Both are intended to preserve the
same mechanism and test invariance to meaning-preserving changes. First
Step Swapped replaces the initiating event while holding the downstream
chain fixed and is treated as a different mechanism under the study
rubric. Middle Step Swapped replaces one intermediate step while
preserving the initiating event and terminal finding.

#### Generation and structural validation.

Variants are generated using claude-sonnet-4-6 at temperature 0.3 and
retained only if they pass deterministic validation against the original
causal chain. Wording Only must preserve all chain steps and regulatory
directions, Wording + Chain must preserve the ordered entities after
alias normalization, and the step-swapped variants must change exactly
one step at the designated position. Constructions that fail these
checks are excluded.

## Appendix D Sensitivity Analyses for Pairwise Comparison Methods

#### Threshold sensitivity and cross-method agreement.

At the selected thresholds of 0.25 for TF–IDF and 0.77 for embeddings,
the three comparison methods achieve 85%–89% raw pairwise agreement and
chance-corrected agreement of $`\kappa\in[0.59,0.74]`$. Sweeping the
TF–IDF and embedding thresholds changes their same/different decisions,
but no evaluated threshold produces complete agreement among the
methods; the highest chance-corrected agreement with another method is
$`\kappa=0.74`$. Thus, the observed differences among the methods are
not attributable to a single threshold setting.

#### Judge-model and presentation-order sensitivity.

On the 180 pairs drawn from the generated hypothesis set, repeating the
full-rubric LLM judgment at temperature 0 in the same presentation order
changes none of the decisions, whereas reversing the order of the two
hypotheses changes 5 decisions (3%). Repeating the comparison with three
judge models yields 96.1%–98.3% pairwise agreement and
$`\kappa=0.86`$–0.94. These results indicate high consistency across
repeated evaluations and judge models, with a small residual dependence
on presentation order.

#### Rubric and order interactions.

We compare the full, step-by-step, and no-rubric prompts on the same
controlled perturbation pairs while holding the judge model,
temperature, sampling procedure, and rendered inputs fixed
(Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Explicit criteria improve sensitivity to causal differences. ‣ 5.2 Measured diversity depends on the equivalence rule ‣ 5 Results ‣ Auditing Pairwise Equivalence Judgments: Self-Critique Effects and Diversity Measurement in Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation")).
Exact repetition in the same order changes no decisions under any
prompt. Presentation-order reversal changes 7 decisions under each
prompt, but the affected pairs differ: two are shared between the full
and step-by-step rubrics, and none are shared with the no-rubric prompt.

## Appendix E LLM-as-a-judge Prompts

### E.1 Critique-engagement judge

The critique-engagement judge decomposes each critique into individual
demands and classifies the proposer’s response to each demand as
conceded, answered, partially addressed, or dropped.

### E.2 LLM-as-a-judge and rubric variants

The LLM-as-a-judge determines whether two hypotheses describe the same
or different mechanism. We present the full rubric used throughout the
pairwise analyses, a step-by-step variant that records component-level
judgments before the overall verdict, and a no-rubric variant that
provides only the comparison task.
````
